title: NOT NULL, DEFAULT, primary keys and UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT
summary: Constraints are invariants the database checks on every write, from every client. NOT NULL and DEFAULT shape columns, a primary key names the row, and UNIQUE (with NULLS NOT DISTINCT since PG 15) guards the real-world identity a surrogate key can't.

examples.title: DEFAULT fills omitted columns; an explicit NULL is not omitted

annotations.note: PRIMARY KEY means NOT NULL plus UNIQUE plus "this is the row's identity": one per table, and the default target of foreign keys. The identity column generates it (previous module).
NOT NULL DEFAULT is the usual pair. The default spares every INSERT from naming the column; NOT NULL stops a later UPDATE from setting it to "no value".
Leave a column nullable only when NULL has a meaning you can name. Here it does: the ticket is unassigned.
Both rows get status 'open'. The DEFAULT keyword asks for the default explicitly, which helps in a multi-row VALUES list where only some rows carry a value.
The ORM trap: a client that always lists every column sends NULL for "not set", so the DEFAULT never fires. Omit the column or write DEFAULT. The error carries SQLSTATE 23502 (not_null_violation).

examples.title: Surrogate keys identify rows; UNIQUE keeps the real-world identity

annotations.note: A natural key is data that already identifies the thing. It reads well wherever it is referenced: users.currency below says TRY with no join. The price is paid when it changes, because every referencing row must change too. ISO codes almost never change; e-mail addresses do.
The identity column makes every row distinct, so the same person signs up twice. A surrogate key answers "which row", never "which person".
The common shape: a meaningless, immutable id for references, and the natural key declared unique next to it.

A UNIQUE constraint takes plain columns only. lower(email) is an expression, so it becomes a unique index, which enforces the same rule. lower() uses the database's case rules: under C.UTF-8, I lowers to i, never to ı (see the pitfalls).
The e-mail address changed and the id did not, so anything pointing at users.id is untouched. With email as the primary key, every referencing row would need the update.

'Ayse.Yilmaz@Example.com' and the stored address have the same lower(), so the index rejects it (SQLSTATE 23505, unique_violation). The error names the index: give constraints and indexes names your error mapping can recognise.

examples.title: UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (PG 15) for optional key columns

annotations.note: By default a unique constraint treats NULLs as distinct, so two "global" theme rows coexist and every lookup of the global default becomes a coin toss. The SQL standard leaves this choice to each database, and they differ.

NULLS NOT DISTINCT makes (NULL, 'theme') equal to (NULL, 'theme') for this constraint only; NULL = NULL in a query is still NULL. Before PG 15 the workaround was a second, partial unique index: (key) WHERE tenant_id IS NULL.
The second global theme row now fails with the same SQLSTATE 23505 as any other duplicate.

use_cases: NOT NULL DEFAULT for status fields, flags and counters, so no code path can leave them unset
Surrogate identity key plus UNIQUE on the natural key: users (email), products (sku), requirements (project_id, code)
Natural primary keys for small, stable, standard codes: ISO 4217 currencies, ISO 3166 countries
NULLS NOT DISTINCT for 'global default plus per-tenant override' tables and other keys with an optional part
strengths: Unlike a check in a Go handler or a zod schema, a constraint also covers psql sessions, migration scripts and the second service that writes the same table
Uniqueness holds under concurrency: two transactions inserting the same e-mail can't both commit, which an application-side SELECT-then-INSERT can't promise
Violations come back with a SQLSTATE (23502, 23505) and the constraint name, so the API can map them to a precise 409 or 422 in one place
weaknesses: Every PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE is a B-tree index that each INSERT and key UPDATE must maintain
A DEFAULT applies only when the column is omitted; clients that always send every column bypass it
Case-insensitive or partial uniqueness needs a unique index, which can't be attached as a table constraint with ADD CONSTRAINT ... USING INDEX
A natural primary key that changes has to be rewritten in every referencing row

pitfalls.title: Sending NULL and expecting the DEFAULT
pitfalls.detail: Only an omitted column or the DEFAULT keyword gets the default. An explicit NULL is stored as NULL, or rejected by NOT NULL.
pitfalls.bad: INSERT INTO tickets (title, status) VALUES ('x', NULL);
pitfalls.good: INSERT INTO tickets (title) VALUES ('x');  -- or VALUES ('x', DEFAULT)

pitfalls.title: Treating the surrogate key as the uniqueness rule
pitfalls.detail: An identity primary key makes every row distinct, duplicates included. Declare UNIQUE on whatever identifies the thing in the real world.

pitfalls.title: Case-insensitive keys under the wrong case rules
pitfalls.detail: lower() follows the database's case rules. StackLab's databases use C.UTF-8, which maps I to i, so lower('IŞIK') is 'işik' and never collides with 'ışık'. When Turkish rules define identity (user names, product names), index the Turkish lowercase. For e-mail addresses the default rules are what you want.
pitfalls.good: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users (lower(username COLLATE "tr-x-icu"));

pitfalls.title: Expecting UNIQUE to reject a second NULL
pitfalls.detail: Under the default NULLS DISTINCT, any number of rows may hold NULL in a unique column. Use NOT NULL, or NULLS NOT DISTINCT on PG 15+.

quiz.q: status is `text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open'`. What does `INSERT INTO tickets (title, status) VALUES ('x', NULL)` do?
quiz.why: An explicit NULL is a value, so the DEFAULT doesn't apply and NOT NULL rejects it. Only an omitted column or the DEFAULT keyword gets the default.

quiz.q: users has `id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY` and `email text NOT NULL`, nothing else. What stops two rows with the same e-mail?
quiz.why: The primary key is on id, which is different for every row. Only a UNIQUE constraint or unique index on email (or lower(email)) prevents the duplicate.

quiz.q: A table has `UNIQUE (tenant_id, key)` without NULLS NOT DISTINCT. How many rows with (NULL, 'theme') can it hold?
quiz.why: NULLs are distinct by default, so the constraint never considers two of these rows equal.

body:
## Concept

A constraint is a rule the database checks on every INSERT and UPDATE, whoever sends
them. The four in this lesson cover most of a table's shape:

- **NOT NULL**: the column always has a value.
- **DEFAULT**: not a constraint strictly, but its partner: the value used when an INSERT
  leaves the column out.
- **PRIMARY KEY**: the row's identity. Unique and not null, one per table, and what
  foreign keys point at by default.
- **UNIQUE**: no two rows share these values. NULLs count as distinct unless you say
  `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` (PG 15+).

A key is either **natural** (data that already identifies the thing: an ISO currency
code, an e-mail address) or **surrogate** (a generated number or UUID with no meaning).
The usual design is a surrogate primary key for references plus a UNIQUE constraint on
the natural key, because a surrogate key by itself never stops a duplicate.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: Bean Validation's `@NotNull` runs in the JVM, for that one application. `NOT NULL`
  runs in the database, for every client, including psql and the next service someone
  writes.
- Go: a struct field always holds a value; an unset `int` is `0` and is sent as `0`. To
  get the column's DEFAULT, the INSERT has to leave the column out. To store NULL, the
  field needs a pointer or a nullable type.
- TypeScript: a nullable column is `string | null` under `strictNullChecks`, and NOT NULL
  is the database's non-optional property. SQL has no `undefined`: a value is either
  sent or the column is omitted.
- Python/JS: a UNIQUE constraint behaves like a set keyed on its columns, except that
  NULL never equals NULL unless you ask for `NULLS NOT DISTINCT`.

## Design notes

Application validation exists for good error messages; the constraint is the guarantee.
Two app instances can both "check that the e-mail is free" and both insert, while a
unique index lets exactly one of them commit. Map the SQLSTATE (23505
`unique_violation`, 23502 `not_null_violation`) to an HTTP status in one place and
let the constraint name pick the message.

Pick natural primary keys only when the value is small, standard and practically never
changes. Everything people can edit (e-mail addresses, requirement codes like REQ-12,
user names) gets a surrogate id plus UNIQUE. A requirements table, for example, keys
on `id` and declares `UNIQUE (project_id, code)`, so renaming REQ-12 touches one row
and every trace link to it survives.

PostgreSQL 18 records NOT NULL as a constraint in `pg_constraint`, with a name such as
`tickets_status_not_null`, and like a CHECK it can now be added `NOT VALID` and
validated later. What NOT NULL enforces is unchanged.
